body_markdown:
In 1978, the Honda Accord must have felt like an alien spacecraft. That was one of my first thoughts when I tooled around in a nearly perfect, 50,000-mile 1978 Accord coupe that American Honda’s PR folks recently dropped by our office.


I was just eight years old and a voracious reader of car magazines when the Accord landed on our shores. Reviewers marveled at the Accord’s obvious quality: The doors made a solid thunk when closed, the turn signal stalk elegantly glided into position, and even the interior plastic trim felt somehow many cuts above the norm.


Chris Stark


The Accord’s retail price was about four grand—cheaper than domestic small cars, yet better equipped. I’ve never driven a Chevy Chevette, an obvious GM competitor to the Honda in the late 1970s, but I did own a[1983 Volkswagen GTI](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/your-handy-1974-84-volkswagen-golf-rabbit-mk1-buyers-guide/) —VW’s economy hatch with a few hot-rod bits—and wow, what a pile of junk it was compared with this Accord. When I drove it the other day, the 48-year-old Honda was still shockingly quiet, smooth, and comfortable. One detail that really stuck out was the power steering pump, which didn’t make that groaning sound you heard so often in domestic cars of the era. Honda, in 1978, was on a different planet. And that turned out to matter enormously—because building a car this good, at this price, set off a chain of events that would consume the car business for the next fifteen years.


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


In the late Seventies, Honda dealers couldn’t keep cars on lots. Customers put their names on waiting lists. Dealerships and the people who controlled how many Accords each dealership received—what the industry calls “allocation”—suddenly found themselves sitting on a gold mine. This was true for Toyota, too, a phenomenon described by John Updike in his terrific novel[Rabbit Is Rich](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0449911829?lv=shuf&channelId=500&plpRedirect=mhFallback) , in which everyman hero Harry Angstrom prospers by selling Toyotas while American gas guzzlers sit unsold. That’s when things got interesting—and ugly.


Chris Stark


Washington noticed. Toyota, Datsun (soon to be rebranded Nissan), and Honda together[had grown from 1.1 million U.S. sales in 1978 to 1.4 million in 1982](https://www.epi.org/publication/the-decline-and-resurgence-of-the-u-s-auto-industry/) . In 1980, Japanese imports occupied more than 20 percent of the U.S. market, while the Big Three lost a record $4.2 billion, their sales plummeting 30 percent below 1978 levels to their lowest point since 1961, according to a[scholarly analysis by Stephen D. Cohen for the National Security Archive](https://nsarchive2.gwu.edu/japan/scohenwp.htm) . Cohen’s dense but fascinating paper explains how the Reagan Administration pressured Japan into what was politely called a Voluntary Export Restraint, or VER. Japan would limit all its auto exports to the U.S. to 1.68 million units a year. It was a quota in everything but name, and it made a scarce product even scarcer. A Honda allocation wasn’t just valuable now. It was precious.


In this environment, some of the most creative corruption the American car business has ever seen blossomed. American Honda’s own executives—the men who decided which dealers got how many cars—began to realize they were sitting on a fortune. What followed was, according to federal prosecutors who eventually brought the case, the largest commercial bribery scandal in U.S. history, with approximately $50 million in cash and goods involved.


The full story was documented by Steve Lynch, a former Honda marketing executive who lived through the era, in his 1997 book[Arrogance and Accords: The Inside Story of the Honda Scandal](https://www.amazon.com/Arrogance-Accords-Inside-Story-Scandal-ebook/dp/B01E7LKSVS/ref=sr_1_1?crid=1TZSU1SHCOX2R&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.-3Gl3lqp5t9kInqqOd4dwQ.riQUVMxxaw9cKd0Zt2vsrXXXP-tt12Yp5rHEfXcsF1Y&dib_tag=se&keywords=arrogance+and+accords+the+inside+story+of+the+honda+scandal&nsdOptOutParam=true&qid=1788954333&sprefix=arrogance+and+acc%2Caps%2C135&sr=8-1) . At 326 pages it is a quick, well-crafted, and jaw-dropping read. According to Lynch, about a third of Honda’s 1000 U.S. dealers participated in the scheme to one degree or another, showering executives with cash, Rolex watches, home renovations, Hong Kong shopping sprees, golf memberships, and college tuition payments. Former executive Jack Billmyer, delivering a line that belongs in a mob movie, famously summed up the culture: “At American Honda, they don’t pay you a million dollars, but you can live like a millionaire.”


Chris Stark


Honda launched an internal review in 1992 and fired a dozen managers, hoping to contain the scandal, but they couldn’t. The scheme fully unraveled in New Hampshire, of all places, when a dealer named Richard Nault filed a lawsuit against American Honda over a wrongful franchise termination. During the proceedings, allegations of criminal wrongdoing surfaced, and the presiding judge referred the matter to federal prosecutors and the FBI. The aforementioned Billmyer, American Honda’s former national sales manager, and Dennis Josleyn, the former West Coast sales manager, were among those convicted in federal court in Concord, New Hampshire, of taking cash and luxury items from dealers in exchange for favorable allocations and coveted new franchises. Billmyer was sentenced to five years in prison. Josleyn got six.


When it was all over, 18 Honda executives had been convicted on federal charges and sentenced to prison, with another ten sales officials found guilty of lesser charges. Dealers who had played by the rules and been starved of inventory eventually won a $329 million civil settlement from Honda, according to court records. I’m re-reading Lynch’s book and it is a page turner!


Chris Stark


Here’s the thing that strikes me now, having just stepped out of that 1978 Accord: None of it would have happened if the car had been mediocre. The bribery, the quotas, the federal prosecutions—it all traces back to how good the cars were. What’s amazing to me is how Honda’s DNA in its core products, the Accord and Civic, has not been corrupted over the decades. Drive a 1995 or a 2025 Accord and you feel immediately that it came from the same company that built the 1978 car: the same obsessive fit and finish, the same sense that every switch and surface was considered rather than just installed. The allocation scandal was about greed. The car itself remained honest throughout.


And that, really, is what makes the car business unlike almost any other industry. It sits at the intersection of engineering, economics, politics, human greed, and genuine passion—sometimes all at once. An engineer in Japan obsesses over the feel of a turn signal stalk, a consumer in Ohio falls in love with the car in which it is installed, Washington and Tokyo end up in trade negotiations over the distribution of the car, and a bunch of white-collar executives end up in jail. Amazing.
